first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this, so I read it properly on the iPad. The opening is lovely. 'The aunt who cried at the aisle' made me smile, because that will be my sister. It's calm and there's no silly slang, so I kept going. I'll be honest though: the photo app is her decision, not mine. What I was really looking for was anything about my mother, whether the children's photos are safe, and who these Wedded Wonderland people are.

journey.quote: A wedding photo app gathers those pictures and videos in one private place, so they don't scatter across a hundred phones and group chats.
journey.reaction: Good, it says 'private'. I don't want the whole family's photos ending up on the internet. Plain words, I understood straight away what the thing is for.

journey.section: Guest photos and your photographer's gallery
journey.quote: Guest photos are a second layer, never a replacement.
journey.reaction: Thank goodness. I was worried she'd try to save money on the photographer by getting everyone to use their phones. This tells me the photographer still matters, and that's money I'm happy to spend.

journey.quote: Older guests may find a new app a hurdle, and international guests on roaming plans may be reluctant to download anything.
journey.reaction: Yes. My mother won't be downloading anything, and nor will half my friends. I'm glad someone thought of us without making us sound hopeless. But it's two lines and then it moves on. It only tells me to use a browser link. Will Mum actually manage a QR code? Is anyone going to help her?

journey.quote: Can a guest upload from the phone's browser, with no app and no account? If not, what does a guest share to sign up?
journey.reaction: That second question is a sensible one. I don't want my email address or my phone number handed to some company I've never heard of. I'll forward this bit to my husband.

journey.quote: Ask how long the album stays online and what happens afterwards, then download and back up well before any deadline.
journey.reaction: Practical. It's what I'd say myself: don't trust them to keep it forever. It tells me to make a copy, which is exactly the sort of thing I'll be nagging her about.

journey.quote: Australia's eSafety Commissioner advises that you should always ask for consent before sharing a photo or video.
journey.reaction: Quoting a government body is reassuring. It reads as though they've checked rather than made it up.

journey.quote: eSafety advises parents to check with other parents before posting, sharing or tagging images that include their children
journey.reaction: This matters to me. My nephew's little ones will be there and their mother is very particular. I'm glad it's spelled out.

journey.quote: The Act does not cover individuals, so it does not apply to photos taken by someone acting in a personal capacity, though state or territory laws may apply in some situations.
journey.reaction: By here I'm reading a legal pamphlet. These paragraphs are long and full of Acts and Commissioners. I had to read this one twice, and I'm still not sure what I'm meant to do with it. The welcome sign line just after it is much more useful.

journey.section: Copyright in photos your guests take
journey.quote: Where someone agrees, for valuable consideration, to have a photograph taken for a private or domestic purpose, which includes a portrait of a wedding party, that person owns the copyright; the photographer can restrain uses outside a purpose made known at the time, and the rule can be changed by agreement.
journey.reaction: That sentence is far too long for an iPad. It also raises a question for me. If I'm the one paying the photographer, does that make me 'that person'? It doesn't say, and it's the kind of thing my husband will ask.

journey.section: Copyright in photos your guests take
journey.quote: In practice, ask a guest before you print, frame or post their photo, and read the usage and copyright clause in your photographer's contract before you sign.
journey.reaction: Finally, the plain version, and it mentions a contract. Good. I'd have liked this at the start of the section, not the end.

journey.section: Questions to ask the venue about internet and data
journey.quote: Ask whether guest Wi-Fi reaches every space you are using, from the ceremony site to the garden, whether it copes with many guests uploading at once, and whether the password can go on your cards.
journey.reaction: Sensible questions for an overseas venue. It shows someone has actually stood at one of these places. It does make me wonder what else I should be asking the venue, like whether Mum can get from the ceremony to the garden, but that's not what this article is about.

journey.section: Guest photos at a destination wedding
journey.quote: Venue questions, guest communication and timing sit more easily with one Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as your single point of contact.
journey.reaction: One person to deal with is what I want. 'Who do I ring?' Apparently this Advisor. But there's no name, no phone number, and nothing about how they work or what it costs. I'm not saying it should all be in an article about photo apps, but I'd want a phone call before anyone sees a cent from us.

journey.section: Planning the rest of the day
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor works in your time zone and stays your single point of contact, start to finish.
journey.reaction: 'Works in your time zone' is the best line in the whole piece for me. If something goes wrong at 2am Italian time, I'd like to know I can reach someone in Melbourne hours. It's the first thing on the page that makes me curious about the company itself.

unanswered_questions: If I'm the parent paying the photographer, who owns the copyright in the professional photos: me, my daughter, or the couple?
Will someone help older guests like my mother upload photos on the night, or is that left to the family?
Who exactly is the Wedded Advisor, and can I speak to them on the phone before anything is booked?
How are Wedded Wonderland's own fees agreed, and is it all in writing and in AUD? (Not covered here.)
Who is responsible if the photo company loses the photos or shuts down before we've downloaded them?

turn_offs_found.quote: The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner treats photos and videos as personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 when a person's identity is clear or could reasonably be worked out. The Act does not cover individuals, so it does not apply to photos taken by someone acting in a personal capacity, though state or territory laws may apply in some situations.
turn_offs_found.why: Long, dense paragraph of legal wording. It's tiring to read on an iPad and I came away unsure what it means for us.

turn_offs_found.quote: Where someone agrees, for valuable consideration, to have a photograph taken for a private or domestic purpose, which includes a portrait of a wedding party, that person owns the copyright; the photographer can restrain uses outside a purpose made known at the time, and the rule can be changed by agreement.
turn_offs_found.why: One enormous sentence. It reads like a contract, not advice for a family.

would_share_with: My husband, for the privacy and copyright parts, with a note asking who owns the photographer's pictures if we're paying
My daughter, back to her, with the welcome sign line underlined and a reminder about Mum and the QR code

cta_reaction.quote: Talk to our Wedded Concierge team when you are ready, and for ideas in the meantime, browse our magazine.
cta_reaction.why: The single point of contact in my time zone appeals to me. But this article is about photo apps, and it tells me nothing about how they handle money, contracts or deposits, which is what I'd need before I'd ring. I'd tap through to see who they are and whether there's a phone number, but my daughter would be the one to enquire.

top_3_changes: Give older guests a little more than two lines, without adding facts. OLD: "Older guests may find a new app a hurdle, and international guests on roaming plans may be reluctant to download anything. A browser upload page removes that friction." NEW: "Older guests, grandparents included, may find a new app a hurdle, and international guests on roaming plans may be reluctant to download anything. A browser upload page removes that friction, so nobody is left out."

Split the long commissioned-photos sentence so it can be read on a tablet. Wording unchanged, only the punctuation. OLD: "which includes a portrait of a wedding party, that person owns the copyright <!-- fact_16 --> <!-- fact_18 -->; the photographer can restrain uses outside a purpose made known at the time <!-- fact_17 -->, and the rule can be changed by agreement. <!-- fact_19 -->" NEW: "which includes a portrait of a wedding party, that person owns the copyright. <!-- fact_16 --> <!-- fact_18 --> The photographer can restrain uses outside a purpose made known at the time. <!-- fact_17 --> The rule can also be changed by agreement. <!-- fact_19 -->"

Break up the dense OAIC paragraph so the practical steps stand apart from the legal background. checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent, 62, reading on an iPad from a link her daughter sent)
No invented brand facts; missing details (fees, phone contact, named person, supplier responsibility) listed as unanswered questions
Suggested edits use exact old/new strings, add no new facts, name no apps and add nothing on fees, commissions, sourcing or vetting of suppliers
HTML comments and image slots treated as invisible for reading (only kept inside edit strings so the edits stay exact)
Scores are 1 to 5 and top_3_changes has no more than 3 items

open_questions.question: A paying parent naturally asks whether she, as payer, is 'that person' under the commissioned-photo rule. Should the writer or SME address who the commissioning party is when a parent pays, or is that out of scope for general information?
Can the closing CTA offer a phone call with a Wedded Advisor? The page doesn't say one is offered, so I haven't proposed that wording.

assumptions: Margaret reads the whole article top to bottom, as her decision behaviour says, even though the topic is mainly her daughter's choice.
The persona card is provisional and not calibrated with CRM, so these reactions reflect assumed rather than observed behaviour.
